claim: Drosophila predominantly employs a modified tripod gait (M-tripod) across all walking speeds.
source: Flies predominantly employ a modified tripod gait that only changes marginally with speed.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The mechanics of a tripod gait can be approximated with the angular and radial spring-loaded inverted pendulum (ARSLIP) model.
source: The mechanics of a tripod gait can be approximated with a simple model – angular and radial spring-loaded inverted pendulum (ARSLIP) – which is characterized by two springs of an effective leg that become stiffer as the speed increases.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting data shown in Figure 6, where ARSLIP provides significantly better fits than SLIP.

claim: The change in stiffness of the spring is mediated by the change in tripod shape rather than a change in stiffness of individual legs.
source: Surprisingly, the change in the stiffness of the spring is mediated by the change in tripod shape rather than a change in stiffness of individual legs.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis in Figure 7C showing that spring constants predicted from geometry closely match optimized values.

claim: Mammals undergo transition from walking to other coordination patterns such as run, trot, or gallop at precise speeds.
source: In insects, changes in interleg coordination with change in speed are strikingly different from mammals: mammals undergo transition from walking to other coordination patterns such as run, trot, or gallop at precise speeds.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about mammalian locomotion for comparison with insect locomotion.

claim: Mammals walk below Froude number of 0.3 while choosing other gaits at higher Fr.
source: Moreover, in mammals, gait transitions measured in terms of speeds relative to their size defined as Froude number (Fr) occur at specific Fr (Alexander, 1989). They walk below Fr of 0.3 while choosing other gaits at higher Fr.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Alexander, 1989.

claim: Insects employ a tripod gait at a wide range of Froude numbers from 0.001 in flies to Fr > 1 in cockroaches.
source: In contrast, insects employ a tripod gait at a wide range of Fr from 0.001 in flies (Biswas et al., 2018), Fr of 0.25 in ants (Reinhardt et al., 2009), and Fr > 1 in cockroaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on different insect species.

claim: When insects change gait, the gait selection appears to be probabilistic, meaning different gaits can be employed at the same speed.
source: Insects do change their gaits (Wendler, 1966); when insects change gait, the gait selection in insects appears to be probabilistic, that is, different gaits can be employed at the same speed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wendler, 1966 and presented as a known characteristic of insect locomotion.

claim: During mammalian walking, the center of mass is at its highest position at mid-stance.
source: During mammalian walking, the CoM is at its highest position at mid-stance, and the horizontal speed of the CoM is lowest at mid-stance (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about mammalian locomotion and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: During mammalian walking, the horizontal speed of the center of mass is lowest at mid-stance.
source: During mammalian walking, the CoM is at its highest position at mid-stance, and the horizontal speed of the CoM is lowest at mid-stance (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about mammalian locomotion and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Running in humans or galloping in quadrupeds displays kinematics characterized by a minimum in CoM height.
source: Running in humans or galloping in quadrupeds displays different kinematics from walking that is characterized by a minimum in CoM height (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about mammalian locomotion and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The SLIP model can explain both walking and running CoM kinematics in mammals.
source: Both the walking and running CoM kinematics can be explained by a simple mechanical model called the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with reference to the SLIP model literature.

claim: In the SLIP model, the mass of the animal is concentrated into a point mass supported by a single, massless effective leg.
source: In the SLIP model, the mass of the animal is concentrated into a point mass, which is supported by a single, massless effective leg (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a definition of the SLIP model illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: During the first half of stance in SLIP, the spring is compressed as the body moves through the stance phase, converting kinetic energy into elastic energy.
source: During the first half of stance, the spring is compressed as the body moves through the stance phase, converting kinetic energy into elastic energy stored by leg muscles and tendons.
evidence: This describes the mechanics of the SLIP model based on established biomechanical principles.

claim: During the second half of stance in SLIP, the stored elastic energy is converted back into kinetic energy.
source: During the second half of stance, the stored elastic energy is converted back into kinetic energy.
evidence: This describes the mechanics of the SLIP model based on established biomechanical principles.

claim: The kinetic energy and speed reach their lowest value at mid-stance in SLIP.
source: Thus, the kinetic energy, and therefore the speed, reaches its lowest value at mid-stance, as does the height in most cases.
evidence: This is a consequence of the SLIP model mechanics described in the text.

claim: Mid-stance minimum in speed and height are observed during running in many different mammals.
source: These mid-stance minimum in speed and height are also observed during running in many different mammals (Blickhan, 1989; Blickhan and Full, 1993; Cavagna et al., 1977; McMahon, 1984; McMahon and Cheng, 1990), making SLIP an effective model for running.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on mammalian running.

claim: SLIP can serve as a model for walking by producing a speed minimum and height maximum at mid-stance when the spring is stiff.
source: More recently, it has been appreciated that SLIP can also serve as a model for walking by producing a speed minimum and height maximum at mid-stance (Figure 1A) when the spring is stiff (Geyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Geyer et al., 2006.

claim: SLIP can serve as a model for running in cockroaches.
source: SLIP can also serve as a model for running in cockroaches.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge from previous studies on cockroach locomotion.

claim: In running cockroaches, the CoM reaches a minimum in speed and height at mid-stance.
source: An elegant series of studies on running cockroaches has shown a striking similarity to mammalian running; in both cases, the CoM reaches a minimum in speed and height at mid-stance (Full and Tu, 1990, Full and Tu, 1991) and can be modeled by SLIP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Full and Tu, 1990 and 1991.

claim: A fly's horizontal speed during walking is at its maximum at mid-stance.
source: However, by its very nature, SLIP cannot generate the CoM kinematics of many insects including Drosophila (Figure 1B) because a fly's horizontal speed during walking is at its maximum at mid-stance (Graham, 1972; Mendes et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Graham, 1972 and Mendes et al., 2013, and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: SLIP cannot generate the CoM kinematics of many insects including Drosophila.
source: However, by its very nature, SLIP cannot generate the CoM kinematics of many insects including Drosophila (Figure 1B) because a fly's horizontal speed during walking is at its maximum at mid-stance (Graham, 1972; Mendes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the incompatibility between SLIP predictions and observed fly kinematics.

claim: An animal walking with a tripod gait can be approximated as a point mass supported by three massless springs or a springy tripod.
source: A qualitative consideration of the mechanics of an animal walking on three legs shows that SLIP might be an oversimplified model: an animal walking with a tripod gait can be approximated as a point mass supported by three massless springs or a springy tripod (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a theoretical model proposed by the authors and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: A springy tripod is stable while SLIP is unstable.
source: A springy tripod cannot be approximated by SLIP because the springy tripod is stable while SLIP is unstable.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument based on the mechanical properties of the two models.

claim: As the CoM moves away from the vertical toward the front of the fly, the front leg compresses and tends to push the fly backward.
source: An animal supported by a single SLIP-like leg will fall. As the CoM moves away from the vertical (say toward the front of the fly), the front leg compresses and tends to push the fly backward (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the mechanics of a springy tripod illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: If the CoM moves back, the hind leg will push it forward, creating restorative forces.
source: Similarly, if the CoM moves back, the hind leg will push it forward. These restorative forces cannot be modeled by SLIP but can be modeled by a simple extension to SLIP through the addition of an angular spring to model restorative forces.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the mechanics of a springy tripod.

claim: The three legs of a tripod act like a single leg whose behavior is described by the ARSLIP model.
source: In other words, the three legs of a tripod act like a single leg whose behavior is described by a new biomechanical model – angular and radial spring-loaded pendulum (ARSLIP; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a theoretical model proposed by the authors and illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: The ARSLIP model can model both cockroach-like and fly-like kinematic patterns.
source: This model would enable the modeling of both the cockroach-like and fly-like kinematic patterns.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the capabilities of the ARSLIP model.

claim: The mechanics of a springy tripod is affected by both the stiffness of individual legs and its geometry.
source: The mechanics of a springy tripod is not only affected by the stiffness of individual legs but also by its geometry (or where the legs are positioned on the ground).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument that is later supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Changes in geometry can be a mechanism to accommodate large variation in speed supported by the tripod gait.
source: Changes in geometry can be a mechanism to accommodate large variation in speed supported by the tripod gait and have the potential to explain why tripod gaits can support a large range of speeds.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors that is later supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: The effect of geometry on mechanics can be modeled by the ARSLIP model through the differential effects of the geometry on the radial and angular spring constants.
source: The effect of geometry on mechanics can also be modeled by the ARSLIP model through the differential effects of the geometry on the two spring constants – the radial and angular spring constants (Figure 1E) – which describe the ARSLIP model.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the ARSLIP model that is later validated with data.

claim: The automated data acquisition system generates positional data with a vertical resolution of 20 μm.
source: The fly's CoM was extracted using the Kanade–Lucas–Tomasi (KLT) (Tomasi and Kanade, 1991) algorithm and produced low-noise estimates of the CoM position; the vertical resolution being 20 μm (see 'Materials and methods', 'Tracking CoM and foothold positions', Video 1), which makes the rhythmic up-and-down movement of the CoM apparent (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method and its resolution.

claim: The stance duration is inversely proportional to speed in Drosophila.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Graham, 1972; Mendes et al., 2013; Pearson, 1976; Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990; Wilson, 1966), the stance duration is inversely proportional to speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2D and citations to previous studies.

claim: The swing duration changes with speed but to a smaller extent than the changes in stance duration.
source: The swing duration also changes with speed but to a smaller extent than the changes in stance duration.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The coordination pattern in Drosophila did not change noticeably as a function of speed.
source: The coordination pattern did not change noticeably as a function of speed (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the gait map data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The normalized delays between the legs of the same tripod were small throughout the entire speed range.
source: The normalized delays between the legs of the same tripod were small throughout the entire speed range; the within tripod delays became even smaller with speed.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The prothoracic leg led the other legs in its tripod with a small but significant negative delay.
source: The prothoracic leg led the other legs in its tripod with a small but significant negative delay consistent with previous observations in cockroaches (Bender et al., 2011; Delcomyn, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3B and citations to previous studies in cockroaches.

claim: The normalized delays across legs in the opposing tripods were 0.5.
source: On the other hand, the normalized delays across legs in the opposing tripods were 0.5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The gait employed by flies during forward walking across the entire range of speeds is close to a tripod.
source: These analyses suggest that the gait – as defined by phase differences between legs – employed by flies during forward walking across the entire range of speeds is close to a tripod.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The delays between legs within a tripod decrease slightly with speed.
source: The delays between legs within a tripod do decrease slightly with speed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The small dependence of delays on speed means that there is no qualitative change in gait.
source: The small dependence means that there is no qualitative change in gait.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing small changes in interleg delays with speed.

claim: The small dependence of gait on speed is consistent with the continuum of coordination patterns observed in a recent study.
source: This small dependence on speed is consistent with the continuum of coordination patterns observed in a recent study (DeAngelis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to DeAngelis et al., 2019.

claim: The phase difference between the tripod legs decreases as the speed increases.
source: As the speed increases, the phase difference between the tripod leg decreases, and the spread of the phase difference also becomes smaller (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: About 4% of steps at very low speeds did not conform to any gait.
source: A small percentage (about 4%) of steps at very low speeds did not conform to any gait, and a few steps had a tetrapod coordination pattern, but an overwhelming majority of the steps have a tripodal coordination.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: The CoM typically reached a maximum horizontal speed at mid-stance.
source: As previously reported for stick insects (Graham, 1985) and Drosophila (Graham, 1972; Mendes et al., 2013), the CoM typically reached a maximum horizontal speed at mid-stance (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A and citations to previous studies.

claim: A slow step is characterized by both a lower initial speed and a smaller speed increase.
source: Figure 4B shows the speed for a slower step. A slow step is characterized by both a lower initial speed and a smaller speed increase.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is a mid-stance maximum in the height of the fly.
source: It is important to note that there is a mid-stance maximum in the height of the fly and that the flies are more erect when they are walking faster (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Flies are more erect when they are walking faster.
source: It is important to note that there is a mid-stance maximum in the height of the fly and that the flies are more erect when they are walking faster (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: The change in speed within a step increased with the average speed during the step.
source: The change in speed within a step increased with the average speed during the step. (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At low walking speed, much of the change in speed was due to the increased initial speed.
source: At low walking speed, much of the change in speed was due to the increased initial speed.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At higher walking speed, the mid-stance increases in speed made a greater contribution.
source: At higher walking speed, the mid-stance increases in speed made a greater contribution (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The distance traveled over the tripod gait cycle increases with speed.
source: The distance traveled over the tripod gait cycle also increases with speed (Figure 4E), and the duration of the tripod gait cycle decreases (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The duration of the tripod gait cycle decreases with speed.
source: The distance traveled over the tripod gait cycle also increases with speed (Figure 4E), and the duration of the tripod gait cycle decreases (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The increase in speed is due to both the greater distance travelled during the step, and faster steps.
source: Thus, the increase in speed is due to both the greater distance travelled during the step, and faster steps.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: The longer and faster steps result both from a faster speed at the beginning of the step and a greater increase in speed during the step.
source: The longer and faster steps result both from a faster speed at the beginning of the step and a greater increase in speed during the step.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The springy tripod potential energy is equivalent to the ARSLIP potential energy for evolution that is close to the midpoint and θ=0.
source: We can show through a formal analysis using a Taylor series expansion of the Lagrangian for the springy tripod (see 'Materials and methods' 'Derivation of the formula relating tripod model to ARSLIP') that springy tripod approximately reduces to the ARSLIP model (Figure 5B). As a reminder, in the ARSLIP model, the three legs of the springy tripod are replaced by a single effective leg with a radial and an angular spring. Specifically, Vtri is equivalent to the ARSLIP potential energy, V (Equation 2), for evolution that is close to the midpoint (rm), and θ=0.
evidence: This is a theoretical derivation presented in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In the ARSLIP model, the mechanics of an animal is controlled by two spring constants, ks and ka, and the natural spring length, R.
source: In this model, the mechanics of an animal is controlled by the two spring constants, ks and ka, which describe the stiffness of the radial and the angular spring, respectively, and the natural spring length, R.
evidence: This is a description of the ARSLIP model parameters.

claim: The angular spring forces switch direction at mid-stance.
source: Importantly, the angular spring forces switch direction at mid-stance, which means that they aid forward progression during the first half of the stance and oppose forward progression during the second half of the stance.
evidence: This is a theoretical property of the ARSLIP model.

claim: The angular spring force pattern is exactly opposite to the pattern created by SLIP.
source: This pattern is exactly opposite to the pattern created by SLIP.
evidence: This is a comparison between ARSLIP and SLIP mechanics.

claim: Depending on whether the leg spring dominates, or the angular spring, one can get a cockroach-like speed minimum or fly-like speed maximum at mid-stance.
source: Depending on whether the leg spring dominates, or the angular spring, one can get a cockroach-like speed minimum or fly-like speed maximum at mid-stance.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the ARSLIP model that is later validated with data.

claim: SLIP fails to describe the horizontal progression of the CoM in Drosophila.
source: However, as reported previously (Biswas et al., 2018), SLIP fails to describe the horizontal progression of the CoM.
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figure 6A and citation to Biswas et al., 2018.

claim: ARSLIP can describe both the horizontal and vertical progression of the CoM in Drosophila.
source: In contrast, ARSLIP can describe both the horizontal and vertical progression of the CoM (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In ARSLIP, the angular spring accelerates the CoM during the first half of the stance phase.
source: In ARSLIP, the angular spring accelerates the CoM during the first half of the stance phase.
evidence: This is a description of the ARSLIP model mechanics.

claim: ARSLIP presented significantly smaller RMSEs for both horizontal and vertical CoM displacements than SLIP.
source: ARSLIP presented significantly smaller RMSEs for both horizontal and vertical CoM displacements than SLIP (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Two linear springs defined by their spring constants – ka and ks – are sufficient to describe the fly's CoM kinematics during a step.
source: That the ARSLIP model describes the CoM kinematics well means that two linear springs defined by their spring constants – ka and ks– are sufficient to describe the fly's CoM kinematics during a step.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful fitting of the ARSLIP model to the data.

claim: The median ks was 0.009 N/m.
source: The median ks was 0.009 N/m.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model fitting.

claim: To support its mass of 1 mg or 10 μN weight, the fly compresses the effective spring by about 1 mm or approximately 50% of its length.
source: This spring constant implies that to support its mass of 1 mg or 10 μN weight, the fly compresses this effective spring by about 1 mm or approximately 50% of its length.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured spring constant and fly mass.

claim: The nondimensional radial spring constant γs is ~2 compared to >10 for humans.
source: The nondimensional radial spring constant γs (see 'Materials and methods' for definition) is ~2 compared to >10 for humans (Antoniak et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison between fly and human data, with citation to Antoniak et al., 2019.

claim: The median ka was 1.1 × 10−8 Nm/radian.
source: The median ka was 1.1 × 10−8 Nm/radian.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model fitting.

claim: The angular spring constant γa was ~0.5, which is like the values obtained in humans.
source: In nondimensional terms, the angular spring constant γa was ~0.5, which is like the values obtained in humans.
evidence: This is a comparison between fly and human data.

claim: Compared to humans, the relative role of angular spring in flies is much larger.
source: Therefore, compared to humans, the relative role of angular spring in flies is much larger.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the relative magnitudes of radial and angular spring constants in flies versus humans.

claim: Most animals increase their walking speed by decreasing the stance duration.
source: Most animals increase their walking speed by decreasing the stance duration (Mendes et al., 2013; Pearson, 1976).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: As the walking speed increases and the stance duration decreases, the vertical oscillations must occur faster by making the effective leg stiffer.
source: As the walking speed increases and the stance duration decreases, the vertical oscillations must occur faster by making the effective leg stiffer (because the time needed for vertical oscillation decreases with increases in spring stiffness).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument based on the mechanics of spring-mass systems.

claim: An increase in stiffness with speed has been observed in humans.
source: This increase in stiffness has indeed been observed in humans (Antoniak et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Antoniak et al., 2019.

claim: As the fly's walking speed increases, γs increases.
source: We found a similar increase in stiffness in flies (Figure 6D). As the fly's walking speed increases, γs, the nondimensionalized version of ks increases.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The nondimensional angular spring constant, γa, increases with speed.
source: The nondimensional angular spring constant, γa, increases as well; this increase accounts for the greater within-step increases in speed observed at higher speed (see Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and relates to observations in Figure 4C.

claim: In bipedal walkers, the only mechanism for increasing the overall stiffness of the system is to increase the stiffness of each leg.
source: In bipedal walkers, the only mechanism for increasing the overall stiffness of the system is to increase the stiffness of each leg.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about bipedal locomotion.

claim: In polypedal walkers such as insects, the geometry of the tripod itself is a parameter that can be adjusted to alter the stiffness of the overall system.
source: In the case of polypedal walkers such as insects, including flies, the geometry of the tripod itself is a parameter that can be adjusted to alter the stiffness of the overall system.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors that is later supported by data.

claim: As L/rm ratio decreases or the tripod becomes narrow and tall, both γa and γs increase.
source: Specifically, in the range of values observed in flies, as L/rm ratio decreases or the tripod becomes narrow and tall, both γa and γs increase (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by theoretical predictions shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The predicted γa and γs derived from the tripod geometry were close to the optimal γa and γs obtained from the best fit to the CoM kinematics.
source: We found that, despite all the simplifying assumptions, the predicted γa and γs derived from the tripod geometry were close to the optimal γa and γs obtained from the best fit to the CoM kinematics (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The similarity between predicted and fitted spring constants is particularly significant because the prediction for all the steps of a given fly was made with a single parameter set while fits were optimized for each step.
source: The similarity between predicted and fitted spring constants is particularly significant because the prediction for all the steps of a given fly was made with a single parameter set while fits were optimized for each step representing a large decrease in the number of parameters.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the results in Figure 7C.

claim: The tripod geometry plays a critical role in governing the spring constants.
source: These results show that the tripod geometry plays a critical role in governing the spring constants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between predicted and fitted spring constants.

claim: The increase in speed is usually reflected as a change in L/rm ratio.
source: Since γa and γs increase with speed (replotted in Figure 7D), we anticipate that the increase in speed is usually reflected as a change in L/rm ratio (Figure 7E), implying that the change in tripod geometry is an important mechanism for the control of speed during walking.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The change in tripod geometry is an important mechanism for the control of speed during walking.
source: Since γa and γs increase with speed (replotted in Figure 7D), we anticipate that the increase in speed is usually reflected as a change in L/rm ratio (Figure 7E), implying that the change in tripod geometry is an important mechanism for the control of speed during walking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 7D and 7E.

claim: The M-tripod gait itself is not fixed but has a small dependence on speed.
source: The M-tripod gait itself is not fixed but has a small dependence on speed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gait analysis data in Figure 3.

claim: The small dependence on speed as well as the increase in duty factor as the speed decreases implies that the average number of legs on the ground at any given time will decrease with speed.
source: This small dependence on speed as well as the increase in duty factor as the speed decreases implies that the average number of legs on the ground at any given time will decrease with speed.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observed changes in gait with speed.

claim: The increase in the number of legs on the ground has been shown to be important for stability.
source: This increase in the number of legs has been shown to be important for stability (Szczecinski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szczecinski et al., 2018.

claim: There is evidence that flies change their gait upon amputation.
source: It is important to note too that our findings do not imply that the flies are only capable of a fixed gait. There is evidence that flies change their gait upon amputation (Isakov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Isakov et al., 2016.

claim: Neither the swing duration nor the swing amplitude changes much as the fly's walking speed changes.
source: Previous studies have shown that neither the swing duration nor the swing amplitude (the distance that a leg travels during the swing) changes much as the fly's walking speed changes (Mendes et al., 2013; Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990; Wosnitza et al., 2013), a result that is confirmed in this study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by data in this study.

claim: Much of the change in speed results from a decrease in stance duration.
source: Much of the change in speed results from a decrease in stance duration (Mendes et al., 2013; Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990; Wosnitza et al., 2013), another result consistent with this study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Increase in walking speed results from an increase in the angular speed of the body about its stance legs.
source: In other words, increase in walking speed results from an increase in the angular speed of the body about its stance legs.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that stance duration decreases while swing amplitude remains constant.

claim: Moving faster requires larger forces from the ground, and a mechanically stiffer system would be able to transmit more forces from the ground to the body.
source: A biomechanical element: moving faster also requires larger forces from the ground, and a mechanically stiffer system (in this case, the mechanical system consists of the fly and the legs that support the fly) would be able to transmit more forces from the ground to the body.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument based on biomechanical principles.

claim: There are two mechanisms by which the system can become mechanically stiffer: either a fly could make each leg stiffer or it could change the geometry of the tripod to make the overall system stiffer.
source: There are two mechanisms by which the system can become mechanically stiffer. Either a fly could make each leg stiffer just as has been shown in humans (Antoniak et al., 2019; Kim and Park, 2011) or it could change the geometry of the tripod to make the overall system stiffer.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument with citation to human studies.

claim: The data is consistent with the idea that changes in the geometry of the tripod are the dominant component by which flies control the stiffness of γa and γs and thereby change their walking speed.
source: The data in Figure 7 is consistent with the second idea that the changes in the geometry of the tripod are the dominant component by which flies control the stiffness of γa and γs and thereby change their walking speed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 7.

claim: Changes in γs allow the fly to adjust the stiffness of its mechanical system to the stance duration; a stiffer γs means shorter time period of oscillation.
source: Changes in γs allow the fly to adjust the stiffness of its mechanical system to the stance duration; a stiffer γs means shorter time period of oscillation.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument based on the mechanics of oscillating systems.

claim: Changing γs through changes in geometry would also change γa.
source: Changing γs through changes in geometry would also change γa.
evidence: This is a consequence of the mathematical relationship between tripod geometry and the two spring constants.

claim: The increase in γa provides a parsimonious explanation for the greater mid-stance maximum in speed observed when the fly walks faster.
source: We regard the changes in γa as an inevitable consequence of the changes in γs; nonetheless, the increase does provide a parsimonious explanation for the greater mid-stance maximum in speed observed when the fly walks faster.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the observed changes in γa.

claim: The control of speed through tripod geometry has never been explored in any insect.
source: To our knowledge, the control of speed through tripod geometry has never been explored in any insect.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: In flies, the L/rm ratio varies between 1 and 2.
source: In flies, the L/rm ratio varies between 1 and 2.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: For three species of stick insects, the L/rm ratio ranges between 2 and 3.
source: We could obtain a rough estimation of the L/rm ratio for a few insects by piecing together information from some manuscripts or by measuring these ratios from the figures in the papers: for three species of stick insects, the ratio ranges between 2 and 3 (Theunissen et al., 2015), wood ants have a L/rm ratio of closer to 1 (Reinhardt and Blickhan, 2014), and cockroaches have a L/rm ratio closer to 6 (Ting et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Theunissen et al., 2015.

claim: Wood ants have a L/rm ratio of closer to 1.
source: We could obtain a rough estimation of the L/rm ratio for a few insects by piecing together information from some manuscripts or by measuring these ratios from the figures in the papers: for three species of stick insects, the ratio ranges between 2 and 3 (Theunissen et al., 2015), wood ants have a L/rm ratio of closer to 1 (Reinhardt and Blickhan, 2014), and cockroaches have a L/rm ratio closer to 6 (Ting et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Reinhardt and Blickhan, 2014.

claim: Cockroaches have a L/rm ratio closer to 6.
source: We could obtain a rough estimation of the L/rm ratio for a few insects by piecing together information from some manuscripts or by measuring these ratios from the figures in the papers: for three species of stick insects, the ratio ranges between 2 and 3 (Theunissen et al., 2015), wood ants have a L/rm ratio of closer to 1 (Reinhardt and Blickhan, 2014), and cockroaches have a L/rm ratio closer to 6 (Ting et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ting et al., 1994.

claim: Large variation in the L/rm ratio will have a large effect on the CoM kinematics within a step.
source: This large variation in the L/rm ratio will have a large effect on the CoM kinematics within a step.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the ARSLIP model.

claim: At low L/rm ratio, when the legs are almost vertical, γs is large in comparison to γa.
source: Given a leg stiffness γ, at low L/rm ratio, that is, when the legs are almost vertical, γs is large in comparison to γa; therefore, the deceleration due to γs as the fly approaches mid-stance cannot be compensated by the acceleration due to γa.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the ARSLIP model equations.

claim: As the L/rm ratio increases, the effects due to γa and γs are comparable for a range of L/rm values.
source: As the L/rm ratio increases, the effects due to γa and γs are comparable for a range of L/rm values.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the ARSLIP model equations.

claim: At very large L/rm ratios, γs again dominates.
source: At very large L/rm ratios, γs again dominates.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the ARSLIP model equations.

claim: Whether the gait is cockroach-like or fly-like depends on the interplay between γa and γs, which in turn depends on the stiffness of individual legs and the geometry of the tripod.
source: These ideas can be formalized by deriving conditions for which the gait is cockroach-like versus fly-like (Appendix): whether the gait is cockroach-like or fly-like depends on the interplay between γa and γs, which in turn depends on the stiffness of individual legs and the geometry of the tripod.
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived in the Appendix.

claim: For a given L/rm, there is a leg stiffness γ above which the kinematics change from a cockroach-like gait to a fly-like gait.
source: For a given L/rm, there is a leg stiffness γ above which the kinematics change from a cockroach-like gait to a fly-like gait (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: The data points for each of the fitted steps for the fly lie above the function that demarcates the two kinematic types.
source: As expected, the data points for each of the fitted steps for the fly lie above the function that demarcates the two kinematic types.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 8A showing that fly data is consistent with fly-like kinematics.

claim: The L/rm ratio for flies and several other insects places them in a regime in which the leg stiffness required for a fly-like gait is at a minimum.
source: Importantly, the L/rm ratio for flies and several other insects places them in a regime in which the leg stiffness required for a fly-like gait is at a minimum (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 8A.

claim: Ants, stick insects, and flies all have fly-like kinematics.
source: Indeed, ants, stick insects, and flies all have fly-like kinematics.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Cockroaches have L/rm values that predispose them toward a mid-stance minimum velocity profile.
source: On the other hand, cockroaches have L/rm values that predispose them toward a mid-stance minimum velocity profile.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical analysis in Figure 8A and known cockroach L/rm values.

claim: At the L/rm ratios observed in flies and other insects such as ants and stick insects, small changes in L/rm will produce a corresponding change in γs.
source: At the L/rm ratios observed in flies and other insects such as ants and stick insects, small changes in L/rm will produce a corresponding change in γs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: At large L/rm ratio, such as those employed by a cockroach, the γs is constant and does not depend on the L/rm ratio.
source: On the other hand, at large L/rm ratio, such as those employed by a cockroach, the γs is constant and does not depend on the L/rm ratio.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: At the large Froude numbers employed by cockroaches, the CoM kinematics is dominated by the angular speed with which the body moves about its leg, and it is rather insensitive to the magnitude of γs.
source: At the large Fr numbers employed by cockroaches, the CoM kinematics is dominated by the angular speed with which the body moves about its leg (Antoniak et al., 2019), and it is rather insensitive to the magnitude of γs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Antoniak et al., 2019.

claim: At lower speeds, the mechanics is dominated by the spring constants γa and γs.
source: On the other hand, and as demonstrated for flies in this study, at lower speeds the mechanics is dominated by the spring constants γa and γs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of fly locomotion in this study.

claim: The strong dependence of mechanics on the L/rm ratio or tripod geometry can explain both why tripod gait can be employed across a range of speeds observed among different insects and that a given insect can control its speed in part by changing the geometry of its tripod.
source: In sum, the strong dependence of mechanics on the L/rm ratio or tripod geometry can explain both why tripod gait can be employed across a range of speeds observed among different insects and that a given insect can control its speed in part by changing the geometry of its tripod.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the theoretical and experimental results.

claim: It has been well known that CoM kinematics for other insects are dramatically different from cockroach and cannot be explained by the SLIP model.
source: However, it has been well known before the recent studies in flies that CoM kinematics for other insects are dramatically different from cockroach (Graham, 1985; Reinhardt and Blickhan, 2014), and cannot be explained by the SLIP model.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: The geometry of the tripod plays an important role in determining the mechanics of the CoM.
source: The development of a general model will be aided by two important insights in this study: first, we show that the geometry of the tripod plays an important role in determining the mechanics of the CoM.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Cockroaches walk with a particularly wide and low tripod where the mechanics are closest to being described by the SLIP model.
source: It appears that cockroaches do walk with a particularly wide and low tripod where the mechanics are closest to being described by the SLIP model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of L/rm ratios and their effect on mechanics.

claim: The wide and low tripod observed for cockroaches appear to be an exception rather than a rule.
source: But the wide and low tripod observed for cockroaches appear to be an exception rather than a rule.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing tripod geometries across different insect species.

claim: At least some of the kinematic variations observed in insects result from differing tripod geometries.
source: The tripod geometries of other insects are different, and as shown in Figure 8, at least some of the kinematic variations observed in insects result from these differing tripod geometries.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical analysis in Figure 8.

claim: The effect of the different tripod geometries can be captured through the ARSLIP model.
source: Second, the effect of the different tripod geometries can be captured through a simple extension of the SLIP model – the ARSLIP model.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study demonstrated through model fitting and theoretical analysis.

claim: The ARSLIP model is simple enough that it retains much of the elegant simplicity that makes SLIP such a powerful model while being better equipped to capture the greater diversity of kinematics observed in insects.
source: The ARSLIP model is simple enough that it retains much of the elegant simplicity that makes SLIP such a powerful model while being better equipped to capture the greater diversity of kinematics observed in insects.
evidence: This is an assessment of the advantages of the ARSLIP model.

claim: The springy tripod presented is a simplification for the actual dynamics of locomotion in insects.
source: It is obvious but still important to note that the springy tripod presented here is a simplification for the actual dynamics of locomotion in insects.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the model.

claim: The springy tripod is a decent model of the fly's walking as shown by its ability to predict the optimized ARSLIP spring constants from geometry.
source: In the case of fly, the springy tripod is a decent model of the fly's walking as shown by its ability to predict the optimized ARSLIP spring constants from geometry (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis in Figure 7C.

claim: The ARSLIP model itself is more general and can model other known features of insect legged locomotion.
source: However, the ARSLIP model itself is more general and can model other known features of insect legged locomotion that we have not considered here:
evidence: This is a statement about the potential broader applicability of the ARSLIP model.
